displayQuote: Once you replace negative thoughts with positive ones, you'll start having positive results

meta.title: Who really said "Once you replace negative thoughts with positive ones, you'll start having positive results"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Dale Carnegie. Quote Investigator traces this line to the epigraph of Willie Nelson's The Tao of Willie (2006). Carnegie wrote a near-miss in 1948.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Once you replace negative thoughts with positive ones, you'll start having positive results'?
meta.ogDescription: Quote Investigator credits Willie Nelson: the line is the epigraph of The Tao of Willie (2006). Dale Carnegie's 1948 book has a similar phrase, not this one.

answer.label: Not Dale Carnegie — actually Willie Nelson
answer.authorDates: b. 29 April 1933 · American singer-songwriter, author of The Tao of Willie
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator ↗ traced this sentence and concluded that Willie Nelson should be credited with it: it is the epigraph of The Tao of Willie: A Guide to the Happiness in Your Heart, written with Turk Pipkin and published by Gotham Books in 2006, on page vii. Dale Carnegie is a genuine near-miss rather than a random famous name — his How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948) says that turning a minus into a plus “will replace negative thoughts with positive thoughts,” which is a different sentence making a related point. Carnegie died in 1955; the aphorism as people share it appears in Nelson’s 2006 book.

source.excerpt: Once you replace negative thoughts with positive ones, you’ll start having positive results.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ investigated this exact sentence and concluded that Willie Nelson should be credited with it, citing The Tao of Willie: A Guide to the Happiness in Your Heart by Willie Nelson with Turk Pipkin, epigraph, page vii, Gotham Books, New York, 2006 — marked verified on paper.

The Carnegie link is real but does not reach this wording: QI cites How to Stop Worrying and Start Living by Dale Carnegie, page 134, Simon and Schuster, New York, 1948 — also verified on paper — for the phrase about replacing negative thoughts with positive thoughts, and presents it as a thematic precursor. A scan of that 1948 Simon and Schuster edition ↗ is catalogued at the Internet Archive.
Negative check on the popular credit: Wikiquote’s Dale Carnegie page ↗ maintains a sourced section specifically for How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1948), and this line does not appear in it.

The book itself checks out independently of QI: Open Library ↗ and the Internet Archive catalogue record ↗ both give Willie Nelson with Turk Pipkin, Gotham Books, New York, 2006, 185 pages — Open Library indexes the edition under ISBN 9781592401970 and records ISBN-10 159240197X.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller passage to quote: the line stands alone on page vii as the book’s epigraph, which is part of why it travels so cleanly. For contrast, the Carnegie sentence people confuse it with is embedded mid-argument — turning a minus into a plus, he writes, “will replace negative thoughts with positive thoughts.”

author.name: Willie Nelson
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: b. 29 April 1933, Abbott, Texas · American singer, guitarist, songwriter & author
author.bio: Willie Nelson is an American singer, guitarist, songwriter, actor and activist, born in Abbott, Texas in 1933 — one of the architects of outlaw country and a founder of Farm Aid. He is also a working author: The Tao of Willie: A Guide to the Happiness in Your Heart (2006), written with his long-time friend Turk Pipkin, is a slim collection of road-tested life advice rather than a memoir. The line people pin on Dale Carnegie is the sentence Nelson chose to open it with.

misattribution.heading: Where the credit goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Quote Investigator opens its investigation on this sentence by naming five possible authors — “Willie Nelson? Dale Carnegie? Norman Vincent Peale? James K. Van Fleet? John C. Maxwell?” — which is a fair map of where the line has been filed. Only one of them wrote it.

items.why: Carnegie is one of the names this line gets misfiled under — Quote Investigator opens its investigation by asking about him — and the misfile has a real seed. Quote Investigator ↗ verified on paper that his How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (Simon and Schuster, 1948) says at page 134 that the attempt to turn a minus into a plus “will replace negative thoughts with positive thoughts.” QI presents that as a thematic precursor, not as this quotation — the wording differs and the “positive results” payoff is absent. Wikiquote’s Carnegie page ↗, which keeps a sourced section for the 1948 book, does not carry the line either.

items.who: Norman Vincent Peale, James K. Van Fleet, John C. Maxwell
items.why: All three appear in QI’s chronology ↗ as writers who circled this thought — Peale in The Power of Positive Thinking, Van Fleet in Hidden Power (1987), Maxwell in Thinking for a Change (2003), where the relevant passage is itself credited to Bob Rotella. None of them is offered as the source of this wording.

items.who: Quote sites that print it with no source at all
items.why: Where the aggregators do get the name right, they still supply nothing to check it against: Goodreads ↗ attributes the line simply “― Willie Nelson,” naming no book, page or year. Sourceless attribution is what lets a line drift onto a more famous name in the first place.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence is Willie Nelson’s, and it has an address: the epigraph on page vii of The Tao of Willie: A Guide to the Happiness in Your Heart, written with Turk Pipkin and published by Gotham Books in 2006, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why this one gets misfiled
lead: This is a rare misattribution with an honest explanation behind it. Most fake Dale Carnegie quotes are pure invention — someone needed a motivational caption and reached for the most famous self-help name available. This one is different: Carnegie really did write a sentence about replacing negative thoughts with positive ones, in How to Stop Worrying and Start Living in 1948. It just isn’t this sentence.

The version that spread — tighter, punchier, ending on “positive results” — is how Willie Nelson opened The Tao of Willie in 2006. It sits alone on page vii as the book’s epigraph, which is exactly the format that travels: no paragraph around it, nothing to trim, ready-made for a poster. Strip the book cover away and the line reads like generic mid-century self-help, so that is where people file it.
context.detailsSummary: The other names in the running
detailsBody: Quote Investigator opens its investigation by listing five candidates: Willie Nelson, Dale Carnegie, Norman Vincent Peale, James K. Van Fleet and John C. Maxwell. All but Nelson turn out to be thematic company rather than sources.

Peale’s The Power of Positive Thinking contains a line about thinking positively setting in motion forces that bring “positive results” — close in vocabulary, different in construction. Van Fleet’s Hidden Power (1987) and Maxwell’s Thinking for a Change (2003) are cited by QI in the same family; Maxwell’s passage there is credited to Bob Rotella, not offered as the aphorism.
The useful takeaway: “replace negative thoughts with positive ones” is a decades-old commonplace of self-help writing. What Nelson supplied was the finished, quotable shape of it.
context.pull: Carnegie wrote something close. The sentence everyone actually shares is Nelson’s.
